title: Anchor Theory, Rebar Theory and the Missing Bridge: A Map of the Design Methods for Post-Installed Bonded Steel in Concrete—Why a Reinforcing Bar May Ignore the Concrete Cone, Why a Threaded Rod May Not, and a Rule for When the Cone Is Relevant
content: Post-installed bonded steel in concrete is designed today by at least six methods: the concrete capacity method of EN 1992-4, the anchorage and lap rules of EN 1992-1-1 with EAD 330087, strut-and-tie models, EOTA TR 069 with EAD 332402, the cover-dependent anchorage of EN 1992-1-1:2023 with its new provisions for post-installed bars, and manufacturer methods; in North America, ACI 318 offers the same split between anchoring (Chapter 17) and development length (Chapter 25). The methods rest on different mechanical models and reach opposite conclusions on the same question. The anchor methods verify the concrete cone for every fastener up to 20 diameters; the reinforcement methods never verify it. A ribbed bar and a threaded rod of equal strength, in the same hole and the same mortar, may therefore be designed to differ by a factor of two to ten, and the boundary between the two treatments is drawn by the name of the steel element rather than by any stated criterion. This paper sets out each method with its rationale, its qualification basis, its field of application and its limits, and identifies the common mechanics beneath them. The concrete cone is a property of the load path: it forms where the tension of the element must return through concrete in tension, and it is absent where that tension is closed by a lap with existing reinforcement, by a compression strut to a proven node, or by hanger reinforcement. The reinforcement methods may ignore the cone because their field of application consists of closed load paths; they are misused, and the cone returns, when they are applied to open ones such as beam-to-column moment connections with straight bars, for which a worked example gives a cone resistance of 18% of the yield force of the bars. Independently of closure, the cone ceases to govern a single fastener at 11 to 18 diameters against steel and 4 to 18 against bond, but never ceases to govern a dense row by depth alone. The paper identifies the bridges that already exist between the two families (TR 069 with ψM,N, EN 1992-4 7.2.1.2(2)e, supplementary reinforcement, rebars designed as fasteners, strut-and-tie proof of nodes) and proposes the one that is missing: an element-neutral rule built on a closure ratio and a dominance ratio , written as a single verification N_Ed ≤ min[N_Rd,s; N_Rd,b; N_Rd,c M,N/(1 − )] whose end points are EN 1992-4 ( = 0) and EN 1992-1-1 ( ≥ 1). Under it a threaded rod and a bar in the same position give the same result; the steel element enters only through bond qualification and, for moment and seismic connections, a ductility requirement. A decision schema summarises the use of every method. A seismic example computed with the author’s software (AAS, ARS) shows the stakes: for one metre of Ø12 bars at 150 mm the anchor route gives 161 kN, 39% of the capacity-design force, while the rebar route anchors the bars for that force with 651 mm of embedment.
